questions.q: Who became the first emperor of Rome?
questions.fact: Augustus, who was born with the name Octavian, became Rome's first emperor in 27 BC.

questions.q: Which wonder of the ancient world was a giant lighthouse in Egypt?
questions.fact: The Lighthouse of Alexandria stood on the island of Pharos and was one of the tallest buildings of the ancient world.

questions.q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World is the only one still standing?
questions.fact: The Great Pyramid was built about 4,500 years ago for the pharaoh Khufu.

questions.q: What were the picture symbols used for writing in ancient Egypt called?
questions.fact: Hieroglyphs could be written left to right, right to left, or top to bottom.

questions.q: Which stone helped experts finally read Egyptian hieroglyphs?
questions.fact: The Rosetta Stone has the same message in three scripts, which helped Jean-François Champollion crack hieroglyphs in 1822.

questions.q: Which young pharaoh's tomb was found almost untouched in 1922?
questions.fact: Howard Carter found King Tut's tomb in the Valley of the Kings, packed with golden treasures.

questions.q: What wedge-shaped writing was invented in ancient Mesopotamia?
questions.fact: Cuneiform was pressed into wet clay tablets with the end of a cut reed.

questions.q: Which river did farming in ancient Egypt depend on?
questions.fact: The Nile flooded every year and left rich black soil behind for growing crops.

questions.q: Which Greek city-state was famous for its tough warriors?
questions.fact: Spartan boys started their military training at about age 7.

questions.q: In which ancient Greek city did democracy first develop?
questions.fact: Athenian democracy began around 508 BC, but only free adult men were allowed to vote.

questions.q: Which Macedonian king built a huge empire before he died at age 32?
questions.fact: Alexander's empire stretched from Greece all the way to the edge of India.

questions.q: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with war elephants to attack Rome?
questions.fact: Hannibal crossed the Alps in 218 BC, and many of his elephants did not survive the cold.

questions.q: What were the fighters who battled to entertain crowds in Roman arenas called?
questions.fact: Many gladiators were enslaved people or prisoners, but the best ones became as famous as sports stars.

questions.q: What is the name of the giant ancient arena in the middle of Rome?
questions.fact: The Colosseum was finished in AD 80 and could hold around 50,000 people.

questions.q: Which Roman leader was killed on the Ides of March in 44 BC?
questions.fact: The Ides of March is another name for March 15.

questions.q: What language did the ancient Romans speak?
questions.fact: Latin is the root of Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian.

questions.q: According to legend, which city was captured by soldiers hiding inside a wooden horse?
questions.fact: The story of the Trojan Horse comes from ancient Greek myths and poems.

questions.q: Who led the Huns in their attacks on the Roman Empire?
questions.fact: Attila was so feared that Romans called him the Scourge of God.

questions.q: Which Mongol leader founded the Mongol Empire in 1206?
questions.fact: At its biggest, the Mongol Empire was the largest connected land empire in history.

questions.q: Which grandson of Genghis Khan started the Yuan dynasty in China?
questions.fact: The traveler Marco Polo wrote about visiting the court of Kublai Khan.

questions.q: Which Italian traveler wrote about his journey to China in the 1200s?
questions.fact: Marco Polo said he spent about 17 years in China working for Kublai Khan.

questions.q: What was the famous network of trade routes between China and the Mediterranean called?
questions.fact: The Silk Road carried silk, spices, ideas and even inventions like paper between East and West.

questions.q: During which Chinese dynasty was most of the Great Wall we see today built?
questions.fact: Most of the wall that tourists visit today was built during the Ming dynasty, which ruled from 1368 to 1644.

questions.q: Who was the first emperor of a united China?
questions.fact: The name China may come from Qin, which is said like "chin".

questions.q: What is the army of clay soldiers buried with China's first emperor called?
questions.fact: Farmers digging a well found it in 1974, and it has more than 8,000 figures.

questions.q: Which Chinese thinker taught about respect, family and good behavior about 2,500 years ago?
questions.fact: The sayings of Confucius were collected by his students in a book called the Analects.

questions.q: Which ancient Chinese general is said to have written The Art of War?
questions.fact: The Art of War is still read today by athletes, business leaders and game players.

questions.q: Which empire built Machu Picchu high in the Andes?
questions.fact: Machu Picchu was built in the 1400s and became world famous after the explorer Hiram Bingham visited it in 1911.

questions.q: What was the capital city of the Aztec Empire?
questions.fact: Mexico City is built on top of the ruins of Tenochtitlan, which sat on an island in a lake.

questions.q: Which civilization built the great pyramid city of Chichen Itza in Mexico?
questions.fact: On the spring and fall equinoxes, shadows make a snake shape slither down the side of its main pyramid.

questions.q: Which Spanish conquistador brought down the Aztec Empire?
questions.fact: Cortés and his local allies captured Tenochtitlan in 1521.

questions.q: Which Spanish conquistador conquered the Inca Empire?
questions.fact: Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532.

questions.q: What was the capital of the Inca Empire?
questions.fact: Cusco is still a busy city in Peru, and some of its streets have walls built by the Inca.

questions.q: What did the Inca use their knotted strings, called quipus, for?
questions.fact: The Inca had no written alphabet, so quipus helped them track numbers like taxes and harvests.

questions.q: Which seafaring raiders from Scandinavia attacked coasts across Europe from about 800 to 1050?
questions.fact: Vikings were also traders and explorers who sailed as far as North America.

questions.q: Which Viking explorer reached North America around the year 1000?
questions.fact: Leif called the land Vinland, and a Viking site has been found in Newfoundland, Canada.

questions.q: Which battle in 1066 led to the Norman conquest of England?
questions.fact: William the Conqueror won the battle and was crowned King of England on Christmas Day 1066.

questions.q: Which long embroidered cloth tells the story of the Norman conquest of England?
questions.fact: The Bayeux Tapestry is nearly 70 meters long and even shows Halley's Comet.

questions.q: What was the deadly plague that swept across Europe in the 1300s called?
questions.fact: The Black Death killed somewhere between a third and half of all the people in Europe.

questions.q: What were the wars fought over the Holy Land between Christian and Muslim armies in the Middle Ages called?
questions.fact: The First Crusade began in 1096.

questions.q: Which French teenager led armies during the Hundred Years' War?
questions.fact: Joan was about 17 when she helped end the siege of Orléans in 1429.

questions.q: How long did the Hundred Years' War between England and France actually last?
questions.fact: The Hundred Years' War ran from 1337 to 1453, with long breaks in the fighting.

questions.q: What was the medieval system where lords gave land to people in return for loyalty and service?
questions.fact: At the bottom of the feudal system were peasants called serfs who worked the land.

questions.q: In the Middle Ages, what was a boy called when he first began training to become a knight?
questions.fact: Pages started training around age 7 and became squires at about 14.

questions.q: What was the time of rebirth in art and learning that began in Italy in the 1300s called?
questions.fact: Renaissance is a French word that means rebirth.

questions.q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
questions.fact: Michelangelo spent about four years, from 1508 to 1512, painting the huge ceiling.

questions.q: Who started the Protestant Reformation by writing his 95 Theses in 1517?
questions.fact: The new printing press helped Luther's ideas spread quickly across Europe.

questions.q: Which English king had six wives?
questions.fact: A rhyme helps people remember their fates: divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived.

questions.q: Which queen ruled England when the Spanish Armada was defeated in 1588?
questions.fact: Elizabeth I ruled for 44 years and never married.

questions.q: Who wrote the play Romeo and Juliet?
questions.fact: Shakespeare also wrote 154 poems called sonnets.

questions.q: What was the name of the London theater where many of Shakespeare's plays were performed?
questions.fact: A rebuilt Globe Theatre opened near the original site in 1997.

questions.q: Which Portuguese explorer reached India by sailing around Africa in 1498?
questions.fact: Vasco da Gama's route let Europeans trade for spices without crossing land.

questions.q: Which country paid for Christopher Columbus's voyage in 1492?
questions.fact: Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Spain agreed to pay for the trip after Portugal said no.

questions.q: What was the name of the ship that carried the Pilgrims to America in 1620?
questions.fact: The Pilgrims founded Plymouth Colony in what is now Massachusetts.

questions.q: What was the first permanent English settlement in North America?
questions.fact: Jamestown was founded in Virginia in 1607.

questions.q: Which English colony is known as the Lost Colony because its settlers vanished?
questions.fact: When help finally arrived, the only clue was the word "CROATOAN" carved into a post.

questions.q: Which Powhatan woman is famous for her connection to the Jamestown colonists?
questions.fact: Pocahontas later traveled to England, where she died in 1617.

questions.q: In what year was the US Declaration of Independence adopted?
questions.fact: It was adopted on July 4, 1776, which is why Americans celebrate on the Fourth of July.

questions.q: In 1773, what did American colonists dump into Boston Harbor to protest taxes?
questions.fact: Colonists threw 342 chests of British tea into the water during the Boston Tea Party.

questions.q: Who made a famous midnight ride in 1775 to warn that British soldiers were coming?
questions.fact: Paul Revere was a silversmith, and other riders also helped spread the warning that night.

questions.q: Who commanded the Continental Army during the American Revolution?
questions.fact: Washington spent the hard winter of 1777 to 1778 with his troops at Valley Forge.

questions.q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States as a gift?
questions.fact: The statue was shipped across the ocean in 350 pieces and dedicated in 1886.

questions.q: Which famous American document begins with the words "We the People"?
questions.fact: The US Constitution was signed in 1787 and is the oldest written national constitution still in use.

questions.q: What are the first ten amendments to the US Constitution called?
questions.fact: The Bill of Rights protects freedoms like free speech and freedom of religion.

questions.q: Which US president bought the huge Louisiana Territory from France in 1803?
questions.fact: The Louisiana Purchase roughly doubled the size of the United States.

questions.q: Which two explorers led an expedition across the American West starting in 1804?
questions.fact: A Shoshone woman named Sacagawea helped guide them and translate.

questions.q: Who was the US president during the American Civil War?
questions.fact: Lincoln was the tallest US president, at about 6 feet 4 inches.

questions.q: Which famous Lincoln speech begins with "Four score and seven years ago"?
questions.fact: The Gettysburg Address is fewer than 300 words long and took about two minutes to give.

questions.q: In what year did the American Civil War end?
questions.fact: The war ended when General Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox Court House in April 1865.

questions.q: Which woman escaped slavery and then led many others to freedom on the Underground Railroad?
questions.fact: Harriet Tubman made about 13 trips and guided around 70 people to freedom.

questions.q: Which man escaped slavery and became a famous speaker and writer against it?
questions.fact: Frederick Douglass taught himself to read even though it was illegal for enslaved people.

questions.q: In which US state did a famous gold rush begin in 1848?
questions.fact: People who rushed there in 1849 were nicknamed the forty-niners.

questions.q: What was the name of the long trail many pioneers used to travel west by wagon in the 1800s?
questions.fact: The Oregon Trail was about 2,000 miles long and took around five months to travel.

questions.q: In what year was the first railroad across the United States completed?
questions.fact: A golden spike was tapped into the track at Promontory Summit, Utah, to finish it.

questions.q: Which woman refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1955?
questions.fact: Her arrest led to the Montgomery bus boycott, which lasted more than a year.

questions.q: Which country did the United States buy Alaska from in 1867?
questions.fact: The US paid about 7.2 million dollars, which works out to about two cents an acre.

questions.q: What 1929 event helped start the Great Depression?
questions.fact: The crash began in October 1929, and millions of people lost their jobs in the years after.

questions.q: Which US president created the New Deal programs during the Great Depression?
questions.fact: Franklin D. Roosevelt is the only US president who was elected four times.

questions.q: Whose assassination in 1914 sparked World War I?
questions.fact: Franz Ferdinand was the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary and was shot in Sarajevo.

questions.q: In what year did World War I end?
questions.fact: The fighting stopped at 11 a.m. on November 11, 1918.

questions.q: What were the long ditches that soldiers fought from in World War I called?
questions.fact: The strip of land between enemy trenches was called No Man's Land.

questions.q: In what year did World War II begin?
questions.fact: The war started in Europe when Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939.

questions.q: Which attack on December 7, 1941 brought the United States into World War II?
questions.fact: Pearl Harbor is a naval base in Hawaii.

questions.q: What was the code name for the Allied invasion of Normandy in 1944?
questions.fact: The landings on June 6, 1944 are known as D-Day.

questions.q: Who was the British prime minister for most of World War II?
questions.fact: Churchill was also a painter and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953.

questions.q: Which Jewish girl wrote a diary while hiding from the Nazis in Amsterdam?
questions.fact: Anne Frank's diary has been translated into more than 70 languages.

questions.q: Which world organization was founded in 1945 to help keep peace between countries?
questions.fact: The United Nations has its headquarters in New York City.

questions.q: What was the long period of tension between the United States and the Soviet Union after World War II called?
questions.fact: It was called cold because the two superpowers never fought each other directly.

questions.q: Which tense standoff in 1962 brought the world close to nuclear war?
questions.fact: The crisis lasted 13 days and ended when the Soviet Union agreed to remove its missiles from Cuba.

questions.q: Who became South Africa's first Black president in 1994?
questions.fact: Mandela spent 27 years in prison before he was freed in 1990.

questions.q: Which Indian leader used peaceful protest to help win independence from Britain?
questions.fact: Gandhi led the famous Salt March in 1930, walking about 240 miles to the sea.

questions.q: In what year did India gain independence from Britain?
questions.fact: India celebrates Independence Day every year on August 15.

questions.q: What was the capital city of the Byzantine Empire?
questions.fact: Constantinople is called Istanbul today.

questions.q: In what year did Constantinople fall to the Ottoman Turks?
questions.fact: The Ottomans used enormous cannons to break through the city's thick walls.

questions.q: Which French leader crowned himself emperor in 1804?
questions.fact: Napoleon was not as short as people joke; he was about average height for his time.

questions.q: In which battle was Napoleon finally defeated in 1815?
questions.fact: Waterloo is in Belgium, and losing there ended Napoleon's rule for good.

questions.q: Which Paris prison was stormed on July 14, 1789, at the start of the French Revolution?
questions.fact: July 14 is now France's national holiday, often called Bastille Day.

questions.q: Which French queen was executed during the French Revolution?
questions.fact: Marie Antoinette was born in Austria and was executed in 1793.

questions.q: Which machine powered factories and trains during the Industrial Revolution?
questions.fact: James Watt made big improvements to the steam engine in the 1760s and 1770s.

questions.q: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
questions.fact: Britain had lots of coal and iron, which helped its factories grow fast in the 1700s.

questions.q: Which queen ruled Britain from 1837 to 1901?
questions.fact: Victoria ruled for 63 years, and the whole era is named after her.

questions.q: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
questions.fact: Amundsen's Norwegian team used sled dogs and beat Scott's British team by about five weeks.

questions.q: What was the name of Ernest Shackleton's ship that was crushed by Antarctic ice?
questions.fact: Every member of the crew survived, and the wreck was found on the seafloor in 2022.

questions.q: Which two climbers were the first confirmed to reach the top of Mount Everest, in 1953?
questions.fact: Hillary was from New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay was a Sherpa from Nepal.

questions.q: In which city was a wall built in 1961 to split it into East and West?
questions.fact: People in Berlin were split from family and friends for 28 years.

questions.q: Which country was ruled by emperors called czars until 1917?
questions.fact: The word czar, also spelled tsar, comes from the Roman name Caesar.

questions.q: Who led the Bolsheviks when they took over Russia in 1917?
questions.fact: After the revolution, Russia became part of the Soviet Union in 1922.

questions.q: Which Soviet leader introduced a policy called glasnost, meaning openness?
questions.fact: Gorbachev won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990.

questions.q: In what year did the Soviet Union break apart?
questions.fact: The Soviet Union split into 15 separate countries, with Russia as the largest.

questions.q: About how long ago was building started on Stonehenge?
questions.fact: Some of Stonehenge's smaller stones were brought from Wales, about 150 miles away.

questions.q: Which Egyptian queen ruled as pharaoh and was often shown wearing a fake beard?
questions.fact: The beard was a sign of a pharaoh's power, so Hatshepsut wore one in statues and pictures.

questions.q: What did ancient Egyptians make their paper-like writing sheets from?
questions.fact: The word paper comes from papyrus, a reed that grew along the Nile.

questions.q: What is preserving a body the way the ancient Egyptians did called?
questions.fact: Egyptians removed the organs and used a salt called natron to dry the body before wrapping it.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek poet is said to have composed the Iliad and the Odyssey?
questions.fact: The Odyssey tells how the hero Odysseus spent 10 years trying to get home after the Trojan War.

questions.q: Which Greek philosopher was a teacher of Alexander the Great?
questions.fact: Aristotle wrote about almost everything, from animals and plants to poetry and politics.

questions.q: Which Greek philosopher was Plato's teacher?
questions.fact: Socrates never wrote any books, so we know his ideas mostly from Plato.

questions.q: At which site in Greece were the ancient Olympic Games held?
questions.fact: The ancient Games were held in honor of Zeus, and a giant statue of him stood at Olympia.

questions.q: Who was the Roman god of war?
questions.fact: The month of March is named after Mars.

questions.q: Who was the king of the gods in ancient Greek myths?
questions.fact: Zeus was said to live on Mount Olympus and to throw lightning bolts.

questions.q: Which Roman emperor ordered a long wall built across northern Britain?
questions.fact: Work on Hadrian's Wall started in AD 122, and parts of it still stand today.

questions.q: What was a large unit of about 5,000 Roman soldiers called?
questions.fact: Roman legionaries could march around 20 miles in a day carrying heavy packs.

questions.q: Which Roman emperor moved the capital to the city of Constantinople?
questions.fact: Constantine named the city after himself in AD 330.

questions.q: In what year is the Western Roman Empire usually said to have fallen?
questions.fact: In 476 the last Western Roman emperor, a teenager named Romulus Augustulus, was removed from power.

questions.q: What is a water-filled ditch around a castle called?
questions.fact: Some moats were dry ditches, and some even had sharp stakes at the bottom.

questions.q: Who wrote The Canterbury Tales in the 1300s?
questions.fact: The Canterbury Tales are stories told by pilgrims on their way to the city of Canterbury.

questions.q: Which legendary outlaw lived in Sherwood Forest and robbed the rich to give to the poor?
questions.fact: Sherwood Forest is in Nottinghamshire, England, and an ancient oak there is called the Major Oak.

questions.q: Which Scottish hero fought the English in the 1290s and was the subject of the film Braveheart?
questions.fact: Wallace won a famous victory at the Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297.

questions.q: In what year did the Great Fire of London happen?
questions.fact: The fire started in a bakery on Pudding Lane and burned for about four days.

questions.q: What was the title of the military rulers who controlled Japan for hundreds of years?
questions.fact: The last shogunate came to an end in 1868 when power went back to the emperor.

questions.q: What was the code of honor that samurai followed called?
questions.fact: Bushido means "the way of the warrior" and valued loyalty, courage and honor.

questions.q: Which warrior queen of the Iceni tribe led a revolt against the Romans in Britain?
questions.fact: Boudica's army burned the Roman town of Londinium, which later became London.

questions.q: Which king of Mali is famous for being one of the richest people who ever lived?
questions.fact: On his trip to Mecca in 1324, Mansa Musa handed out so much gold that its price dropped in Cairo.

questions.q: Which city in Mali was a great center of trade and learning in the 1300s and 1400s?
questions.fact: Timbuktu's old libraries held thousands of handwritten books on science, math and law.

questions.q: Which ancient African kingdom built pyramids in what is now Sudan?
questions.fact: Sudan has more ancient pyramids than Egypt, though they are smaller and steeper.

questions.q: Which stone city in southern Africa gave its name to a modern country?
questions.fact: Its stone walls were built without any mortar holding the stones together.

questions.q: Who made the first solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic Ocean, in 1927?
questions.fact: Lindbergh flew from New York to Paris in about 33 and a half hours in his plane, the Spirit of St. Louis.

questions.q: What 1863 order by President Lincoln declared enslaved people in the Confederate states to be free?
questions.fact: Slavery was fully ended in the US by the 13th Amendment in 1865.

questions.q: Which Spanish explorer became the first European to see the Pacific Ocean from the Americas, in 1513?
questions.fact: Balboa crossed the jungles of Panama to reach the Pacific coast.

questions.q: Which city was the first to be hit by an atomic bomb in war?
questions.fact: The bomb was dropped on August 6, 1945, and a second hit Nagasaki three days later.

questions.q: Which nurse became famous for caring for soldiers in the Crimean War?
questions.fact: Florence Nightingale was called the Lady with the Lamp because she checked on soldiers at night.

questions.q: Who led the revolution that took power in Cuba in 1959?
questions.fact: Fidel Castro led Cuba for almost 50 years.

questions.q: Which empire lasted from about 1299 to 1922 and was ruled by sultans?
questions.fact: At its largest, the Ottoman Empire controlled lands in Europe, Asia and Africa.

questions.q: What were the kings of ancient Egypt called?
questions.fact: The word pharaoh comes from an Egyptian phrase meaning "great house".

questions.q: Which ancient people of Mesopotamia created the first known writing system?
questions.fact: The Sumerians started writing more than 5,000 years ago, mostly to keep track of trade.

questions.q: Which ancient king of Babylon created one of the oldest written sets of laws?
questions.fact: Hammurabi's laws were carved on a tall black stone pillar that is now in a museum in Paris.

questions.q: What do we call the time before people kept written records?
questions.fact: Most of what we know about prehistory comes from tools, bones and cave paintings.

questions.q: Which cave in France is famous for animal paintings about 17,000 years old?
questions.fact: Lascaux was found in 1940 by teenagers following their dog.

questions.q: Which war from 1950 to 1953 was fought between North and South in an East Asian country?
questions.fact: The Korean War ended with an armistice, not a peace treaty, so the two sides never officially made peace.

questions.q: Which long war in Southeast Asia did the United States pull its troops out of in 1973?
questions.fact: The war ended in 1975 when North Vietnam captured Saigon, now called Ho Chi Minh City.

questions.q: Which ancient statue in Egypt has the body of a lion and the head of a human?
questions.fact: The Great Sphinx of Giza is about 73 meters long and was carved from one huge piece of rock.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to become prime minister of the United Kingdom?
questions.fact: Margaret Thatcher became prime minister in 1979 and was nicknamed the Iron Lady.

questions.q: Who was the first US president to live in the White House?
questions.fact: John Adams moved in in 1800, before the building was even finished.

questions.q: In 1893, which country became the first self-governing nation to let women vote in national elections?
questions.fact: A petition for women's voting rights in New Zealand was signed by about 32,000 people.

questions.q: In what year did the 19th Amendment give women in the United States the right to vote?
questions.fact: Women had campaigned for the right to vote for more than 70 years before it passed.

questions.q: Which ancient civilization built the planned city of Mohenjo-daro?
questions.fact: Mohenjo-daro had covered drains and brick houses about 4,500 years ago.

questions.q: Which Indian emperor turned to Buddhism and peace after a bloody war?
questions.fact: The lion statue on top of one of Ashoka's pillars is now India's national emblem.

questions.q: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal?
questions.fact: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

questions.q: Which king united the Hawaiian Islands under one rule?
questions.fact: Kamehameha I brought all the islands under his rule by 1810.

questions.q: Which British captain mapped the east coast of Australia in 1770?
questions.fact: Cook sailed on a ship called the Endeavour.

questions.q: In what year did the First Fleet of British ships arrive in Australia?
questions.fact: Australia Day on January 26 marks the day the First Fleet arrived at Sydney Cove.

questions.q: Which Zulu king built a powerful kingdom in southern Africa in the early 1800s?
questions.fact: Shaka changed how Zulu warriors fought by using short stabbing spears and new formations.

questions.q: Which dictator led Nazi Germany during World War II?
questions.fact: Hitler's Nazi regime murdered six million Jewish people in the Holocaust.

questions.q: What was the line of forts that France built along its border with Germany before World War II?
questions.fact: German armies went around the Maginot Line by going through Belgium in 1940.

questions.q: From which French beach town were more than 300,000 Allied soldiers rescued by boat in 1940?
questions.fact: Hundreds of small private boats, like fishing boats and yachts, helped with the rescue.

questions.q: What machine did Germany use to send secret coded messages in World War II?
questions.fact: Enigma had rotors that scrambled each letter, and its settings changed every day.

questions.q: Which US general led the Allied forces on D-Day and later became president?
questions.fact: Eisenhower was nicknamed Ike and served two terms as president.

questions.q: The most famous US Marine code talkers of World War II spoke which language?
questions.fact: The Navajo code was never broken by the enemy during the war.

questions.q: Which US president resigned in 1974 because of the Watergate scandal?
questions.fact: Nixon is the only US president who has ever resigned.

questions.q: Which US president was assassinated in Dallas in 1963?
questions.fact: Kennedy was 43 when he took office, the youngest person ever elected US president.

questions.q: Who was the first US president to be impeached?
questions.fact: Andrew Johnson was impeached in 1868 and kept his job by just one vote in the Senate.

questions.q: Which US president is the teddy bear named after?
questions.fact: On a 1902 hunting trip, Roosevelt refused to shoot a bear that had been tied up, and a toymaker named a bear after him.

questions.q: Which US president was a Hollywood movie actor before getting into politics?
questions.fact: Ronald Reagan acted in more than 50 films before becoming governor of California.

questions.q: Who was the first African American president of the United States?
questions.fact: Barack Obama was born in Hawaii and was elected in 2008.

questions.q: Which three-day battle in 1863 was a turning point of the American Civil War?
questions.fact: Around 50,000 soldiers were killed, wounded or captured at Gettysburg in Pennsylvania.

questions.q: Who was the top general of the Confederate army in the American Civil War?
questions.fact: After the war, Lee became president of a college in Virginia.

questions.q: Where did the British army surrender in 1781, ending the main fighting of the American Revolution?
questions.fact: The French navy helped trap the British army at Yorktown, Virginia.

questions.q: During which war did British troops burn the White House?
questions.fact: First Lady Dolley Madison saved a famous portrait of George Washington before the fire in 1814.

questions.q: What was the forced removal of the Cherokee people from their homelands in the 1830s called?
questions.fact: Thousands of Cherokee people died on the long journey west to what is now Oklahoma.

questions.q: Which Texas mission was the site of a famous battle in 1836?
questions.fact: Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie died defending the Alamo, and "Remember the Alamo!" became a battle cry.

questions.q: Which 1954 Supreme Court case ruled that separating schools by race was against the Constitution?
questions.fact: The decision overturned the idea of "separate but equal" in public schools.

questions.q: Which 6-year-old girl became the first Black student at an all-white school in New Orleans in 1960?
questions.fact: US marshals walked Ruby Bridges to school every day to keep her safe.

questions.q: What was the disaster in the 1930s when huge dust storms swept across the Great Plains called?
questions.fact: Poor farming methods and drought let the wind blow away the topsoil from millions of acres.

questions.q: Which island in New York Harbor processed millions of immigrants arriving in America?
questions.fact: About 12 million immigrants passed through Ellis Island between 1892 and 1954.

questions.q: In which city did the first Ferris wheel spin at the 1893 World's Fair?
questions.fact: The first Ferris wheel was about 80 meters tall and was built to rival the Eiffel Tower.

questions.q: What nickname is given to the 1920s in America, a time of jazz music and flappers?
questions.fact: Jazz, radio and movies became hugely popular during the Roaring Twenties.

questions.q: What was the US ban on making and selling alcohol from 1920 to 1933 called?
questions.fact: Prohibition led to secret bars called speakeasies and a rise in gangsters like Al Capone.

questions.q: Which British ocean liner was sunk by a German submarine in 1915?

questions.q: Which treaty officially ended World War I in 1919?
questions.fact: It was signed in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles near Paris.

questions.q: Which world peace group was formed after World War I but failed to stop World War II?
questions.fact: The United States never joined the League of Nations.

questions.q: Who was the fascist dictator of Italy during World War II?
questions.fact: Mussolini called himself Il Duce, which means "the leader".

questions.q: Which huge World War II battle in the Soviet Union lasted from 1942 to early 1943?
questions.fact: Stalingrad was one of the bloodiest battles in history and a turning point against Germany.

questions.q: Which naval battle in June 1942 was a major turning point in the Pacific?
questions.fact: At Midway, the US Navy sank four Japanese aircraft carriers.
